motivation: In 2009 Miyasaka and co-workers showed that organometal halide perovskites, CH3NH3PbI3 and CH3NH3PbBr3, can absorb light and generate photocurrent in solar cells. In 2012 Park and co-workers, and independently Snaith and co-workers, built solid-state perovskite cells. Snaith also showed that the perovskite carries charge itself over long diffusion lengths, so it works as a true thin-film semiconductor and not only as a sensitizer. Power conversion efficiency rose from about 4% to above 26% within fifteen years, faster than any other photovoltaic material. Perovskite-silicon tandems now exceed the single-junction silicon limit. The work showed that a solution-processed, defect-tolerant semiconductor can match crystalline materials in optoelectronic quality, and it opened new physics of ionic-electronic transport and exciton behaviour. As with gallium nitride, patient materials work on an unexpected compound is becoming a technology for large-scale, low-cost, sustainable energy.
